title: Shortest Slice Holding the Top Count
statement:
The degree of an array is the highest number of times any single value appears in it. You get a non-empty array nums.

Return the length of the shortest contiguous slice of nums whose degree is the same as the degree of the whole array.

examples.why: Both 5 and 2 appear three times, so the degree is 3. Covering every 5 needs indexes 0 to 6 (length 7), but every 2 fits in indexes 1 to 5 (length 5). Picking the first value with the top count is not enough.
Every value appears once, so the degree is 1, and a single element already has degree 1.
The 4s sit at both ends, so the slice must span the whole array.

hints: A slice with the full degree must contain every copy of some value that has the top count. Why is it enough to look only at those values?
For a value v, the shortest slice holding all its copies runs from its first index to its last index.
In one pass, record for each value its count, first index and last index. Among values with the top count, take the smallest last − first + 1.

explain.intuition:
If the whole array has degree d, a slice with degree d must hold all d copies of some value that appears d times. A slice cannot hold more copies than exist, so it must catch every one of them.

The tightest slice catching every copy of v runs from its first appearance to its last. So the answer is the shortest such span among the values that reach the top count. One pass collecting count, first and last index per value is all you need.
steps: Walk nums once. For each value, increase its count, record its first index if new, and update its last index.
Track the highest count seen, the degree.
For each value whose count equals the degree, compute last − first + 1.
Return the smallest of those lengths.
pitfalls: Using the first value that reaches the top count. Another value with the same count may be packed tighter, as in the first example.
Returning the degree instead of the slice length.
Breaking ties wrongly when updating on the fly: when a value ties the current degree, keep the shorter span, not the newer one.

complexity.space: O(k), where k is the number of distinct values

solutions.title: Grow every slice until it reaches the degree
solutions.idea: Compute the degree. Then from each start, extend the slice and count values until one count hits the degree.

solutions.title: First index, last index, count
solutions.idea: One pass records count and first index per value. Update the answer whenever a value's count beats or ties the degree.

followups: Return the slice itself, and if several have the shortest length, the leftmost one.
Values arrive as a stream. Can you report the answer after every new value in O(1)?
